claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.statement: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.

operationalizations.text: Estimate each apical cell's growth rate, interdivision interval, pre-division shape, and wall orientation, then test whether the growth-to-division ratio predicts the stated transverse, oblique, and axial regimes.

Record cell shape immediately before division and the plane that is used: transverse in markedly oblong cells, oblique when the cell is a little more than a hemisphere, and longitudinal when it is less than a hemisphere. That mapping, in cells whose shape was set by the growth-to-division interval, would support the claim; planes uncorrelated with those shape classes would refute it.

obstacles: Suitable apical-cell series for mosses, liverworts, ferns, and algae are limited.
Polarity and tissue stress may confound the growth-rate ratio.
Shape is partly defined by the growth-to-division ratio, so that half of the wording is close to a description of the cell that is about to divide.
The three-way rule was stated for moss, liverwort, fern and algal apical cells, which these Arabidopsis volumes only approximate.

roles: Mother-cell shapes and daughter walls for a proxy test of the shape-to-plane map

roles: Meristem cells with geometry just before and after division

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claims.statement: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.

operationalizations.text: Compare survival, developmental stage, skeletal-rod mineralization and arm length between control and calcium-depleted sea-urchin larvae. The claim is supported by viable stage-matched larvae lacking rods and long arms specifically under calcium depletion.

In published lime-free versus normal seawater rearings of echinoid embryos, score skeletal-rod presence, larval-arm length and survival. Suppression of rods and arms with continued development supports the claim; normal skeletons, or death rather than skeleton-less development, refutes it.

obstacles: A dedicated open replication dataset may not exist.
Lime-free water can cause physiological effects beyond skeleton loss.
The rearings are reported as figures in papers, not as a reusable open table of larvae, treatments and phenotypes.
Apparently healthy is loosely defined, and the published experiments cover a few echinoid species rather than skeleton-forming organisms generally.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
roles: Searchable public study repository for experimental supplements and larval images.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
claims.statement: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.

operationalizations.text: Compare SSU rDNA molecular phylogenies and single-specimen barcoding against traditional morphospecies and morphogenera in Peneroplis and other variable Foraminifera to test whether distinct named morphospecies/genera share identical or conspecific genotypes.

Compare named morphospecies and genera using genomic delimitations, environmental time series and within-lineage shell morphometrics, especially in Peneroplis. Morphological forms repeatedly intergrading within one reproducing lineage would support the claim; stable genetically distinct lineages would refute it.

Compare morphometric clusters with genetic clusters for genera Thompson treats as variable, especially Peneroplis and planktonic groups with many named forms. The claim is supported where single genetic lineages occupy several named species or genera and morphology shifts within a life cycle; it is refuted where those names correspond to stable, reciprocally monophyletic lineages.

obstacles: Genetic barcoding has sequenced only a fraction of described foraminiferal morphospecies, and in many groups cryptic genetic species outnumber morphospecies rather than the reverse.
Type material and sequence records are rarely linked to the same individuals.
The phrase 'temporary manifestations' can mean plasticity or life-cycle stages.
Peneroplis, the example in the text, has far less public genetic and culture data than planktonic globigerinids.
Cryptic species make the opposite error from ecophenotypes, so a single global test will not have one answer.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
claims.statement: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.

operationalizations.text: Measure the congruence (e.g., Robinson-Foulds distance or phylogenetic signal of shell geometric parameters) between traditional morphology-based classifications of Foraminifera and independent molecular phylogenies.

For traits with an independently supported physical generative model, quantify homoplasy by mapping form similarity onto molecular phylogenies. Excess similarity among distant relatives under shared physical regimes would show that form alone is unsafe evidence of kinship; close correspondence with independent trees would weaken the claim.

Predict genetic or stratigraphic relatedness from shell-shape similarity and compare that prediction with one based on molecular characters. The empirical core is supported if shape neighbors are often distant on sequence trees; it is weakened if shape distance remains a reliable predictor of relatedness after the physically forced characters are removed.

obstacles: The second half of the claim is methodological and normative ('compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny'), though its empirical premise of widespread homoplasy in physically constrained forms is testable.
The claim is conditional on first demonstrating physical control.
Taxonomic classification uses many characters, not form alone.
How much discordance is enough to 'revise the canons' of classification is a judgment, not a threshold in the claim.
Shape-based names enter both the morphological distances and the labels on many sequences.

roles: Supplies molecular sequence data across Foraminifera to compare genetic clades against classical morphology-based families and genera.
Sequence data for phylogenies independent of morphology.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claims.statement: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.

operationalizations.text: For dated growth-zone series, test whether increments align reliably with independent seasonal or diel markers and compare externally forced versus endogenous reaction-diffusion models. Finding internally generated periodicity or poor alignment would refute the assumption that visible rings necessarily record external cycles.

For scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains with known-age or known-environment series, test whether zone counts match day, season or other external periods. Zones that form without a matching external cycle support the claim that periodicity need not be external; a universal match would refute that caution.

obstacles: Different structures have different ring-forming mechanisms.
Environmental covariates and internal rhythms can be correlated.
An endogenous oscillator can still lock to an external cycle, so agreement does not prove external cause.
Starch grains and most bones are poorly represented next to commercial fish otoliths and bivalve or coral bands.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
roles: Public environmental and sclerochronological time-series data can link growth increments to external conditions.
Published sclerochronology and otolith series that pair increment measurements with age or environmental time series.

claims.label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines
claims.statement: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.

operationalizations.text: Use developmental imaging and preserved carapaces to test whether successive retained exuviae adhere as nested layers, project beyond prior margins and generate fitted logarithmic growth lines. Comparison with fully moulting branchiopods would test the incomplete-moult mechanism.

On Estheria and similar conchostracans, test whether surface lines are edges of retained moults, visible in section as stacked carapaces, and whether the outline is a logarithmic spiral of small angle. Stacked retained valves support the incomplete-moult mechanism; a single accreted sheet with growth lines would refute it.

obstacles: Estheria is a historical taxonomic name.
Static carapaces may not distinguish retained moults from continuous secretion.
External lines alone cannot separate retained moults from true shell accretion; that needs sections, which are mostly in papers.
Estheria has been split among several modern genera, so the specimen set has to be delimited carefully.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
claims.statement: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.

operationalizations.text: Map discrete shell architectures (e.g., uniserial, biserial, planispiral, trochospiral, keeled globorotaliid) onto molecular and stratophenetic phylogenies of Foraminifera to test for statistically significant convergent (homoplastic) origins of identical morphotypes across independent lineages.

Map quantified shell forms onto independently inferred molecular and fossil phylogenies and count repeated origins of near-identical morphologies. Multiple distant lineages converging beyond uncertainty would support the claim; forms restricted to single clades would refute it.

Place shell-shape classes on molecular and stratigraphic trees and count independent origins of the same form. Repeated origins of indistinguishable tests in distant clades or separated time intervals would support the claim; a single origin for each form, with similarity tracking relatedness, would refute it.

obstacles: What counts as an 'identical form' depends on the morphological resolution chosen (overall chamber arrangement vs fine wall ultrastructure).
Sparse molecular sampling and uncertain fossil placement.
Identical form requires an explicit morphometric tolerance.
Many benthic genera are still classified by the shell form whose homology is in question.
Molecular trees are dense for planktonic clades and sparse for the long-ranging benthic groups.

claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.label: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claims.statement: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.

operationalizations.text: Segment cells, vacuoles, and nascent spicules in 3D developmental images and test whether deposition follows interfaces and whether interface geometry predicts spicule geometry.

In sponges and radiolaria, record whether mineral is laid down on cell or vacuole boundaries and whether spicule geometry follows those boundaries. Systematic siting on interfaces, with spicule branches tracking junction lines, would support the claim; intracellular initiation away from boundaries would refute it.

obstacles: Mature scans do not identify the developmental interface.
Open developmental volumes cover few sponge and radiolarian taxa.
Isolated-spicule collections omit the cells and vacuoles whose boundaries are the claimed template.
A static section cannot tell whether the boundary preceded the spicule or formed around it.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
roles: Open volume electron microscopy suitable for localizing mineral deposits relative to cellular interfaces.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Public 3D scans for comparative mature spicule geometry.

claims.label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry
claims.statement: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.

operationalizations.text: Using independently inferred cephalopod phylogenies and stratigraphy, test whether spiral angle alone predicts ancestor-descendant order or primitiveness after accounting for size and clade. Frequent convergence and poor temporal prediction would support the warning against inference from angle alone.

Compare spiral angle with phylogenetic distance or ancestral states estimated without using coiling as a character. If angle does not predict which form is ancestral or intermediate, the claim that it is not evidence of ancestry is supported; a robust phylogenetic signal would refute that denial.

obstacles: Independent fossil phylogenies remain uncertain.
The phrase 'no valid evidence' is methodological rather than a simple empirical frequency claim.
Ammonoid cladograms have often used coiling, so a fossil test can become circular.
No evidence of ancestry is an epistemic claim: a weak correlation need not count as valid support, and the threshold is a judgement.
